Thank you, Chair. I'll be presenting the African group's position. On the definition of cross-border tax disputes, The African group supports the direction adopted in the co-leads paper, namely the decision not to define cross-border tax disputes through a narrow or exhaustive legal definition, but instead to rely on common objective features that allow such disputes to be identified in practice. This approach is both pragmatic and consistent with the group's broader commitment to ensuring that the dispute resolution framework remains flexible, inclusive, and responsive to the realities of developing countries. The Africa Group considers that cross-border tax disputes should be understood as disputes that arise between two or more states. Our understanding is that such dispute arises when a taxpayer resident in one jurisdiction engages in a transaction or business activity involving another jurisdiction, and the taxpayer is dissatisfied with the tax treatment in that jurisdiction. It will not, therefore, include disputes between a tax authority and its resident. We also agree with the delegate from Portugal that the resolution process should be a government-led process. It should also relate to the interpretation or application of the framework convention and its protocols, ensuring that the dispute resolution system remains anchored in the agreed multilateral rules. We also think that disputes should include disputes concerning transfer pricing, profit allocation, and permanent establishment issues, which represent the most frequent and complex sources of disagreement between tax administrations and which have significant implications for developing countries' taxing rights. By focusing on these shared characteristics, rather than attempting to craft a rigid definition, the Co-Leads approach avoids unnecessary legal complexity and ensures that the dispute resolution mechanism can accommodate the wide variety of factual scenarios that arise in cross-border taxation. This flexibility is particularly important for developing countries whose administrative capacities and legal systems vary widely and may face disputes that do not fit narrowly into narrow definitional categories. As to question D on the no treaty situation, the co-lead has proposed that the Conference of Parties may develop best practices for resolving disputes in non-treaty situations, and the African group wishes to express concerns with this proposal being included within the protocol. this the basis for our concerns is that there is an absence of a common legal basis which means that there is no shared substantive framework on which to anchor such dispute resolution. Attempting to resolve such disputes multilaterally risks undermining domestic sovereignty and creating inconsistent outcomes. Disputes arising without a treaty should be handled strictly under domestic law and the African group therefore supports excluding best practice development for non-treating disputes from the protocol. Thank you.
